title: Episode 255: Alexander Graham Bell: The Harmonic Telegraph, 'Mr. Watson, Come Here', and the World Connected
description:
The extraordinary life and boundless humanitarian curiosity of Alexander Graham Bell: the Scottish-born teacher of the deaf who transformed human communication forever with the invention of the telephone. Inspired by his deaf mother and wife Mabel Hubbard, Bell sought to develop a harmonic telegraph to transmit multiple musical tones over a single wire, culminating on March 10, 1876, in the immortal words spoken to his assistant: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Founding the Bell Telephone Company, pioneering tetrahedral kites, designing record-breaking hydrofoil boats, co-founding the National Geographic Society, and developing the metal detector to save President Garfield, Bell lived a life of insatiable scientific wonder. Discover the teacher and inventor who united the human family.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series explores the voice that bridged oceans and continents: the Scottish-born educator of the deaf whose compassion and acoustic genius gifted humanity the telephone. Here is George with the life of Alexander Graham Bell.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SOUND OF SILENCE IN EDINBURGH: 1847 TO 1870
Born in March 1847 in Edinburgh, Scotland, Alexander Graham Bell was born into a family profoundly obsessed with human speech, elocution, and vocal acoustics. His grandfather was a celebrated actor and speech authority in London; his father, Alexander Melville Bell, invented 'Visible Speech' —a revolutionary phonetic system of typographic symbols showing the exact physical positions of the tongue, lips, and palate required to produce any spoken human sound. Young 'Aleck' was deeply influenced by his beloved mother, Eliza Grace Bell, an accomplished painter and pianist who became almost completely deaf during his childhood: Aleck learned to converse with her by speaking in low, resonant vibrations pressed directly against her forehead, developing a deep, lifelong reverence for the acoustic mechanics of speech and hearing. At age twelve, noticing the slow, tedious manual work of de-husking wheat at a neighbor's flour mill, Aleck constructed a rotary machine combining wire brushes and rotating paddles that cleaned wheat efficiently, winning his first taste of mechanical invention. When both of his brothers tragically died of tuberculosis within three years, his heartbroken parents resolved to save their surviving son's fragile lungs, packing their belongings in 1870 and immigrating to the clean, crisp air of Brantford, Ontario, Canada, before young Aleck moved south to Boston. Young Aleck's Edinburgh home was a bustling laboratory of elocution, where his father demonstrated Visible Speech to visiting linguists from Oxford and Edinburgh universities. The family's relocation to the heights of Tutelo Heights in Brantford, Ontario, provided Aleck with a peaceful sanctuary where he studied the acoustic anatomy of the human ear and voice.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: TEACHING THE DEAF AND THE BOSTON LABORATORY: 1871 TO 1874
In 1871, twenty-four-year-old Bell opened a private school in Boston for training teachers of deaf-mute students, later being appointed Professor of Vocal Physiology at Boston University. Bell possessed a gentle, charismatic pedagogical genius: using his father's Visible Speech system, he taught deaf children who had never heard a sound how to speak with clear, natural pronunciation. Among his private pupils were George Sanders, a five-year-old born deaf, and Mabel Hubbard, an intelligent, graceful fifteen-year-old who had lost her hearing to scarlet fever as a toddler. Mabel would become the love of Bell's life, his wife of forty-five years, and his greatest intellectual champion. Supported financially by Mabel's wealthy father Gardiner Greene Hubbard and Thomas Sanders, Bell spent his nights experimenting in an attic workshop on Court Street in Boston. Bell was obsessed with developing a 'harmonic telegraph'—a device capable of sending multiple telegraph messages simultaneously down a single wire by tuning tuned steel reeds to vibrating musical frequencies, hoping to break Western Union's monopoly on electronic communication. Bell's pedagogical success with deaf children in Boston earned him the admiration of prominent philanthropists, who recognized that his phonetic system unlocked language for children previously condemned to silence. Mabel Hubbard's intelligence, artistic grace, and lip-reading mastery inspired Bell's deepest acoustic inquiries, transforming his commercial ambitions into a personal crusade of love.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE PLUCKED REED AND THE LIQUID TRANSMITTER: 1875 TO 1876
On the sweltering afternoon of June 2, 1875, while testing his harmonic telegraph apparatus with his skilled young machinist Thomas Watson, an accidental breakthrough occurred. Watson was in an adjoining room adjusting a steel reed that had become stuck to an electromagnet; when Watson plucked the reed with his finger to free it, Bell heard a faint, distinct 'twang' resonate through the receiver in his own room. Bell sprinted into Watson's workshop, shouting: 'What did you do? Don't touch anything!' Bell realized that the vibrating steel reed had generated an undulating electric current that mimicked the physical shape of a sound wave—the very secret to transmitting articulate human speech over a wire. Filing his landmark patent application in February 1876—issued as U.S. Patent 174,465, frequently called the most valuable patent in history—Bell constructed an improved liquid transmitter using a metal rod dipping into an acid solution. On the evening of March 10, 1876, in his boardinghouse room at 5 Exeter Place, Bell accidentally spilled battery acid on his trousers and spoke into the cone transmitter the immortal words: 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Forty feet away in Watson's bedroom, Watson heard the words crisp and clear through his earphone. Watson rushed into Bell's room shouting: 'I heard you! I could hear the words!' The accidental plucking of the stuck steel reed by Thomas Watson in June 1875 proved that an undulating current could transmit the complex harmonics of human vocal chords without interruption. The historic words spoken to Watson on March 10, 1876, were born of an accidental acid spill, turning a minor laboratory mishap into the most famous spoken sentence in electronic history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PHILADELPHIA CENTENNIAL AND THE EMPEROR OF BRAZIL: JUNE 1876
In late June 1876, Bell traveled to the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition to demonstrate his telephone to the international judging panel, which included British physicist Sir William Thomson and Emperor Dom Pedro II of Brazil. It was late on a blistering Sunday afternoon, and the exhausted judges were preparing to leave without inspecting Bell's humble table beneath a stairway in the Education Building. Suddenly, Emperor Dom Pedro recognized Bell: the monarch had visited Bell's school for the deaf in Boston years earlier and admired his pedagogical work. Greeting the young inventor warmly, Dom Pedro agreed to test the apparatus. Bell took the transmitter at the far end of the gallery, five hundred feet away, and spoke into the wire. Dom Pedro held the receiver to his royal ear, jumped back in absolute astonishment, and cried out in Portuguese: 'My God, it talks!' Sir William Thomson tested the telephone and declared it 'the most wonderful thing in America'. The dramatic royal demonstration became an international sensation, splashing Bell's name across world newspapers and transforming the telephone from a scientific curiosity into an unstoppable global industry. Dom Pedro's dramatic reaction at the Centennial Exposition shocked the gathered international scientists, who had previously dismissed Bell's table as an insignificant academic display. Sir William Thomson's glowing public endorsement in the London Times validated Bell's breakthrough, triggering immediate European demand for telephone licenses and demonstration apparatus.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY AND THE PATENT WARS: 1877 TO 1888
In July 1877, Bell, Watson, Hubbard, and Sanders formed the Bell Telephone Company, while Bell married his beloved Mabel Hubbard, presenting her with almost all of his shares in the infant corporation as a wedding gift. Western Union, recognizing that the telephone threatened their entire telegraph empire, launched a vicious counterattack: hiring Thomas Edison and Elisha Gray to design rival telephone apparatus and claiming that Gray had invented the telephone first. For a decade, the Bell Company fought over six hundred separate patent lawsuits all the way to the United States Supreme Court. In every single court case, Bell was completely vindicated: his immaculate laboratory notebooks and precise scientific testimony proved beyond all doubt that he had conceived the undulating continuous current before any other human being. By 1888, the American Bell Telephone Company—which later became the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, AT&T—had constructed a sprawling web of telephone lines connecting cities, transforming business, journalism, and personal life across the globe. The ten-year legal war against Western Union and rival claimants was documented in thousands of pages of court transcripts, establishing Bell's flawless ethical conduct and scientific priority. The expansion of the Bell system laid the foundation for modern telecommunications networks, uniting distant cities into an interconnected, real-time commercial marketplace.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE METAL DETECTOR AND THE TRAGEDY OF PRESIDENT GARFIELD: 1881
Following his financial independence, Bell's restless scientific curiosity exploded in all directions. In July 1881, when President James A. Garfield was shot by assassin Charles Guiteau, doctors were unable to locate the bullet lodged deep in the President's body, probing the wound with unsterilized fingers and causing severe infections. Desperately seeking to save the President's life, Bell worked around the clock in his Washington laboratory, designing an electromagnetic induction balance —the world's first modern metal detector. Bell brought the apparatus to the White House and swept it across the dying President's abdomen, hearing a faint buzzing sound. Tragically, Garfield's physician Doctor Willard Bliss refused to allow Bell to search the left side of the body and neglected to inform him that Garfield was lying on a mattress made with coiled steel wire springs, which distorted the magnetic balance. Garfield died in September, but Bell's metal detector was successfully adapted for military surgery during the Boer War and World War I, saving thousands of wounded soldiers on battlefields around the world. Bell's electromagnetic induction balance used sensitive telephone receivers to detect variations in magnetic fields, demonstrating that audio technology could revolutionize diagnostic surgery. Although Garfield died from septic poisoning, Bell's metal detector paved the way for modern radiographic and surgical metal detection instruments used across global hospitals.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: BADDECK, TETRAHEDRAL KITES, HYDROFOILS, AND THE ENDURING LEGACY
In his later years, Bell established a majestic summer estate named Beinn Bhreagh overlooking the Bras d'Or Lake on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia. Bell turned his estate into a hotbed of experimental science: pioneering tetrahedral kites capable of lifting human passengers, co-founding the Aerial Experiment Association with Glenn Curtiss that achieved the first powered airplane flight in the British Empire in 1909, and designing the revolutionary HD-4 hydrofoil boat that shattered the world water speed record in 1919 at seventy miles per hour. Bell also co-founded the National Geographic Society, serving as its second president and championing the magazine's iconic photographic exploration of world cultures. Yet Bell always viewed himself first and foremost as a teacher of the deaf: until his death in 1922, he maintained a close, affectionate friendship with Helen Keller, who dedicated her autobiography to him. When Alexander Graham Bell was laid to rest atop his mountain in Nova Scotia, every one of the thirteen million telephones in North America went completely silent for one solemn minute—a silent tribute to the man who gave humanity its voice across the earth. Beinn Bhreagh became a center of multidisciplinary wonder, where Bell experimented with sheep breeding, water distillation, tetrahedral architecture, and record-breaking hydrofoil racing boats. The nationwide one-minute telephone silence observed during Bell's funeral was a fitting, poignant tribute to the humanitarian educator who united the voices of humankind. Today, the global network of telecommunications that connects billions of human souls across continents traces its direct lineage back to the gentle Scottish teacher and his harmonic dreams.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 256: The Wright Brothers—Orville and Wilbur, the Kitty Hawk Dunes, and the Conquest of the Air. Until then, stay curious.
